Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $S\subseteq M$ be a Cauchy set
([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c)): every
inextendible causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ has
$\gamma^{-1}[S]=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$ of exactly one element. Then:

**(a)** there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\delta:[a,b]\to M$
with $\delta(a)=\delta(b)$; in particular $S$ is achronal and acausal, and
the three sets $I^-(S)$, $S$, $I^+(S)$ are pairwise disjoint with
$$M=I^-(S)\;\sqcup\;S\;\sqcup\;I^+(S);$$
moreover for $x\notin S$ one has $x\in I^+(S)$ if and only if some point of
$S$ chronologically precedes $x$;

**(b)** $S$ is closed in $M$;

**(c)** for every $p\in S$ there are a chart $(U,x)$ of the kind produced by
[[lem-gr-dominating-cone-bounds]] clauses (a) and (d) around $p$, with
$x(p)=0$ and the supplier constants $K\ge1$ and $c=16$, and numbers $a,\rho,\eta>0$ with $\sqrt c\,\rho+\eta<a$ and
$W:=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times B_\rho(0)\bigr)\subseteq U$ such that for every
$z\in B_\rho(0)$ the coordinate vertical line
$L_z=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times\{z\}\bigr)$ meets $S\cap W$ in exactly one
point $x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$, and
$$|\varphi(z)-\varphi(z')|\le\sqrt c\,|z-z'|\qquad(z,z'\in B_\rho(0)),$$
with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $|\varphi(z)|\le\sqrt c\,|z|<a$. The cylinder $W$ may be chosen inside any prescribed neighborhood of $p$. Consequently the maps
$z\mapsto x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$ form a topological atlas on the closed set
$S$, making $S$ a topological $3$-manifold in the subspace topology whose
inclusion into $M$ is a topological embedding.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let causal
curves be those of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Convergent ends are extendible.** Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the general absolutely continuous endpoint argument in this clause. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a future
causal curve and suppose $b:=\sup I<\infty$ and $\gamma(t)\to x\in M$ as
$t\to\sup I$. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a future causal curve
$\tilde\gamma$ defined on $I\cup[b,b+\varepsilon)$ whose restriction to $I$
is $\gamma$. Consequently a future-inextendible causal curve whose domain is
bounded above does not converge at its upper end, and the dual statement
holds at the past end.

**(b) Maximal geodesics have no limit.** Let $(p,v)\in TM$ with $v\ne0$ and
let $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$, as supplied by
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (a). Then
$\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ does not converge to any point of $M$ as $t\to\sup I_{p,v}$
or as $t\to\inf I_{p,v}$ (where convergence at an infinite end means
convergence as $t\to+\infty$ or $t\to-\infty$ respectively).

**(c) Segments lie on inextendible causal curves.** Let $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to M$
with $t_0<t_1$ be a future causal curve, or a past causal curve. Then there
is an inextendible causal curve $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ (same direction as
$\gamma$ in the case at hand) and a strictly increasing affine map
$\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to J$ with $\hat\gamma\circ\rho=\gamma$. In particular, any
two distinct points $p,q\in M$ with $p\le q$ and $p\ne q$ lie on a common
inextendible causal curve, and likewise for the past relation.

**(d) Cauchy sets are acausal.** Every Cauchy set of
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c) is acausal in
the sense of clause (b) of that definition.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $V\subseteq U\subseteq M$ be open
subsets with the induced metric and time orientation, and let
$\gamma:I\to U$ be a future causal curve
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]) that is inextendible in the
Lorentzian manifold $U$: $\gamma$ does not converge to any point of $U$ as its
parameter tends to either end of $I$ (clause (d) of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], read with ambient set $U$). Let $J$
be a connected component of
$$\gamma^{-1}[V]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in V\}.$$
Then $\gamma|_J$, regarded as a future causal curve in the Lorentzian manifold
$V$ with the restricted fields, is inextendible in $V$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Let $X$ be a set and write $\mathcal{P}(X)$ for its power set. A **topology** on
$X$ is a family $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ such that

- **(T1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$ and $X \in \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T2)** $\bigcup \mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{T}$ for every $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T3)** $U \cap V \in \mathcal{T}$ for all $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$.

A **topological space** is a pair $(X, \mathcal{T})$ consisting of a set $X$ and
a topology $\mathcal{T}$ on it; the elements of $X$ are its **points**. When only
one topology is in play we write $X$ for the pair; when several are, the topology
is always named.

The members of $\mathcal{T}$ are the **open** sets of $(X,\mathcal{T})$. A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed** when its complement $X \setminus F$ is open, and
**clopen** when it is both open and closed. By (T1) both $\varnothing$ and $X$
are clopen. *Open and closed are not opposites*: a set may be neither, and it may
be both, so "not open" is never a synonym for "closed".

**Finite intersections, and the empty one.** Axiom (T3) is stated for two sets
because that is all that is ever needed: if $n \ge 1$ and
$U_1, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{T}$, then $U_1 \cap \dots \cap U_n \in \mathcal{T}$
follows by iterating (T3) $n-1$ times. The intersection of the **empty** family
of subsets of $X$ is $X$, since the condition "lies in every member of the empty
family" is vacuous; that case is covered by (T1) rather than by (T3), which is
one of the two reasons $X \in \mathcal{T}$ is demanded outright. The other is
that (T2) alone gives only $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$.

**The closed sets, and the dual axiomatisation.** Put
$\mathcal{C} := \{\, X \setminus U : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\}$, the family of closed
sets. Then

- **(C1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{C}$ and $X \in \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C2)** $\bigcap \mathcal{D} \in \mathcal{C}$ for every **nonempty**
  $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C3)** $C \cup D \in \mathcal{C}$ for all $C, D \in \mathcal{C}$.

Conversely, if a family $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ satisfies (C1),
(C2) and (C3), then $\mathcal{T} := \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$
is a topology on $X$ whose closed sets are exactly the members of $\mathcal{C}$.
So a topology may be presented equally well by its open sets or by its closed
sets, and this library uses whichever is shorter.

*Both directions are one computation, and it is carried out here rather than
assumed.* The map $U \mapsto X \setminus U$ is an involution of
$\mathcal{P}(X)$, hence a bijection, and it carries the two De Morgan identities

$$X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing), \qquad X \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing)$$

term by term into each other. Given (T1)–(T3): $\varnothing = X \setminus X$ and
$X = X \setminus \varnothing$ lie in $\mathcal{C}$, which is (C1); for nonempty
$\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ the family
$\mathcal{S} = \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{D} \,\}$ lies in $\mathcal{T}$
and $\bigcap \mathcal{D} = X \setminus \bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is closed by (T2),
which is (C2); and $C \cup D = X \setminus ((X \setminus C) \cap (X \setminus D))$
is closed by (T3), which is (C3). Given (C1)–(C3) the same three lines run
backwards, the empty-union case $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$ being supplied
by (C1) rather than by (C2); and $\{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$ has
$\mathcal{C}$ as its family of complements because complementation is an
involution.

**Comparison of topologies.** If $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ are
topologies on the same set $X$ and $\mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_2$, then
$\mathcal{T}_1$ is **coarser** than $\mathcal{T}_2$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ is
**finer** than $\mathcal{T}_1$; the comparison is **strict** when the inclusion
is. Inclusion is a partial order on the set of topologies on $X$
([[def-partial-order]]), and it is not a total one: two topologies on the same
set may be incomparable.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
globally hyperbolic time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), and let
$t$ be the volume time function of [[thm-gr-volume-time-function]]. Then
there exist a smooth function $T:M\to\mathbb R$ and, with $\nabla T$ the
gradient of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], the
following hold.

**(a)** $T$ is a temporal function in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (e): smooth,
$g(\nabla T,\nabla T)<0$ and $g(\nabla T,N)>0$ everywhere.

**(b)** Every level set $S_c:=T^{-1}(c)$, $c\in\mathbb R$, is a Cauchy
hypersurface ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clauses (a)
and (c)): it is a spacelike embedded hypersurface and every inextendible
causal curve meets it in exactly one parameter value. In particular $T$ is
surjective.

**(c)** Along every inextendible future-directed causal curve
$T\to+\infty$, and along every inextendible past-directed causal curve
$T\to-\infty$.

**(d)** The vector field $X:=\nabla T/g(\nabla T,\nabla T)$ is smooth,
future-directed timelike, satisfies $X(T)=1$, and is complete
([[def-complete-vector-field]]): every maximal integral curve of $X$ is
defined on all of $\mathbb R$, so by
[[prop-a-vector-field-is-complete-if-and-only-if-its-flow-is-global]] its
flow $\Phi:\mathbb R\times M\to M$ is a global smooth flow
([[def-local-and-global-flow]]).

**(e)** The map $\Psi:\mathbb R\times S_0\to M$, $\Psi(s,z):=\Phi(s,z)$, is
a diffeomorphism and $T(\Psi(s,z))=s$ for all $(s,z)$; equivalently $M$ is
foliated by the Cauchy hypersurfaces $S_c$, each flow line meeting each level
exactly once.

**(f)** Put $\beta:=-1/g(\nabla T,\nabla T)$, a smooth positive function, and
$h_T:=g+\beta\,dT\otimes dT$. Then $g=-\beta\,dT\otimes dT+h_T$;
$h_T(X,\cdot)=0$; and $h_T$ restricted to $\ker dT$ is a smooth Riemannian
metric, so the decomposition $T_pM=\mathbb RX_p\oplus\ker dT_p$ is
$g$-orthogonal with $g(X,X)=-\beta$. Consequently the pullback of $g$ by the
diffeomorphism $\Psi$ has no mixed terms,
$$\Psi^*g=-(\beta\circ\Psi)\,ds^2+h,\qquad h_{(s,z)}(v,w):=g_{\Phi(s,z)}\bigl((d\Phi_s)_zv,(d\Phi_s)_zw\bigr),$$
a sum of a negative definite one-dimensional form and the smooth family of
Riemannian metrics induced on the levels.

Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ be a development of the given data
([[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)), write

is a development of the same data for $i=1,2$

Let $x$ be a set. By [[lem-the-power-set-of-a-set-is-a-set]] there is exactly one
set whose elements are precisely the subsets of $x$
([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]); it is the **power set** of $x$, written
$\mathcal{P}(x)$. Thus $z \in \mathcal{P}(x)$ holds if and only if
$z \subseteq x$, and in the class notation of the page,

$$\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}.$$

Let $\varphi(z, \bar p)$ be a formula of the language of set theory
([[def-language-of-set-theory]]) in which the variable $y$ does not occur free.
The **Separation instance** for $\varphi$ is the sentence

$$\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,\bigl(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p))\bigr).$$

The **Axiom Schema of Separation** is the collection of all these sentences, one
for each such $\varphi$. In words: for any parameters $\bar p$ and any set $x$,
there is a set $y$ whose elements are exactly the elements $z$ of $x$ for which
$\varphi(z,\bar p)$ holds.

It is a schema and not a single axiom because $\varphi$ ranges over the formulas
of the language, of which there are infinitely many, and the language provides no
way to quantify over them.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the actual maximal-common/no-boundary suppliers and the countable atlas/partition constructions. Let
$(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ and $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ be developments of the same
data ([[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)), write
$\Sigma:=j(\Sigma)$ and $\Sigma':=j'(\Sigma)$, and let $(U,\varphi)$ be their
maximal common development
([[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]] clause (b),
[[lem-gr-maximal-common-development]]). Let
$Z:=(M\sqcup M',\tau)$ be the topological disjoint union with canonical
inclusions $\iota_M:M\to Z$, $\iota_{M'}:M'\to Z$, and define a relation $\sim$ on
$Z$ by: $z\sim w$ when $z=w$, or $z=\iota_M(p)$ and $w=\iota_{M'}(\varphi(p))$ for
some $p\in U$, or $z=\iota_{M'}(p)$ and $w=\iota_M(\varphi^{-1}(p))$ for some
$p\in\varphi(U)$. Let $Q:=Z/{\sim}$ with quotient map $\pi:Z\to Q$ and
quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]]). Then:

**(a)** $\sim$ is an equivalence relation; $\pi\circ\iota_M:M\to Q$ and
$\pi\circ\iota_{M'}:M'\to Q$ are injective, continuous and open, hence
homeomorphisms onto the open subsets $(\pi\circ\iota_M)(M)$ and
$(\pi\circ\iota_{M'})(M')$, which cover $Q$;
$(\pi\circ\iota_M)(U)=(\pi\circ\iota_{M'})(\varphi(U))=(\pi\circ\iota_M)(M)\cap(\pi\circ\iota_{M'})(M')$;
and $Q$ is Hausdorff.

**(b)** $Q$ carries a unique structure of a second countable smooth
four-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) making $\pi\circ\iota_M$ and
$\pi\circ\iota_{M'}$ diffeomorphisms onto open subsets; a unique smooth Lorentzian metric $\bar g$ and matter fields $\bar\psi$ making both maps isometries preserving all matter fields. Their future cones determine a unique future-cone orientation on $Q$. There exists a smooth future timelike representative $\bar N$ of those cones, making both maps time-orientation preserving; this auxiliary vector field is not unique. These satisfy the field equations of the data on $Q$, and
$\bar j:=\pi\circ\iota_M\circ j$ is an embedding of $\Sigma$ with induced data
$(h,K,\psi_0)$, so $(Q,\bar g,\bar N,\bar j,\bar\psi)$ is a development of the
data; moreover every causal curve in $Q$ that is inextendible in $Q$ meets
$\bar j(\Sigma)$ in exactly one parameter value.

**(c)** $\Psi:=\pi\circ\iota_M$ and $\Psi':=\pi\circ\iota_{M'}$ are data-fixing
development embeddings of $M$ and $M'$ into $Q$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (c).

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ and $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ be developments of the same data
in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a),
with $\Sigma:=j(\Sigma)$. Then there exist $U^*\subseteq M$ and
$\psi^*:U^*\to M'$ such that:

**(a)** $(U^*,\psi^*)$ is a common subdevelopment of $M$ and $M'$ in the sense
of [[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]] clause (a);

**(b)** for every common subdevelopment $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ and $M'$ one has
$U\subseteq U^*$ and $\psi^*|_U=\varphi$; in particular $(U^*,\psi^*)$ is a
maximal common development in the sense of clause (b) of that definition, and
it contains $j(\Sigma)$;

**(c)** uniqueness: if $(U^\dagger,\psi^\dagger)$ also satisfies (a) and (b),
then $U^\dagger=U^*$ and $\psi^\dagger=\psi^*$.

**Data.** Fix $\kappa>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, a smooth three-manifold $\Sigma$ without boundary, a smooth Riemannian metric $h$ and smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $K$. The normal convention is $K(V,W)=g(\nabla_Vn,W)$ for the future unit normal. Specify one fixed covariant matter model, consisting of a finite list of smooth tensor fields $\psi$, fixed equations $\mathcal E(g,\psi)=0$ and a fixed stress expression $\mathcal T(g,\psi)$, with pullback by local diffeomorphisms commuting with the equations and stress. Fix its complete smooth Cauchy data $d$: these determine all independent matter initial variables, not only the normal stress projections. Initial tensors with normal directions are specified on the abstract bundle $\mathcal V=\mathbb R\nu\oplus T\Sigma$ with metric $g_0(a\nu+X,b\nu+Y)=-ab+h(X,Y)$. In a development, identify $a\nu+X$ with $an+dj(X)$.

An admissible fixed coupled model is one satisfying the complete initialization, hyperbolic reduction, recovery and comparison hypotheses of [[thm-gr-local-geometric-development]], or a specified independent local existence and uniqueness reduction such as the dust branch below. The same fixed model, complete data and admissibility conditions are used in every comparison and at every restart. Admissibility includes the applicability of its supplied complete-data local existence and geometric uniqueness theorem to the data realized on each spacelike restart surface of the compared solutions. This must be checked for the actual model and surface; it is not inferred from stress conservation. This class includes the following four concrete branches; they do not exhaust it.

1. **Vacuum:** no matter fields, $\mathcal T=0$, and empty matter data.
2. **Scalar field:** fix one smooth potential $V$ and one normalization $K_\phi>0$. The field is $\varphi$, its equation is $\Box_g\varphi-V'(\varphi)=0$, its stress is the expression in [[def-gr-scalar-field-matter-model]] clause (c), and its complete data are $(\varphi_0,\pi_0)$ with $\pi_0=n(\varphi)|_\Sigma$. The fixed potential has no sign restriction ([[thm-gr-scalar-field-local-evolution]]).
3. **Strict barotropic fluid:** fix a smooth EOS $P:J\to\mathbb R$ on an open interval with $\epsilon+P(\epsilon)>0$ and $0<P'(\epsilon)<1$. The fields are $\epsilon\in J$ and future unit velocity $u$, the stress is $(\epsilon+P(\epsilon))u^\flat\otimes u^\flat+P(\epsilon)g$, and the equations are the continuity and Euler equations of [[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]] clause (c), with this fixed EOS. Complete data are $(\epsilon_0,v_0)$, where $\epsilon_0:\Sigma\to J$ and $h(v_0,v_0)<1$, equivalently the bundle velocity $U_0=(1-h(v_0,v_0))^{-1/2}(\nu+v_0)$. No small-tilt restriction is imposed ([[thm-gr-barotropic-fluid-local-evolution]]).
4. **Geodesic nonnegative dust:** the fields are an energy-coefficient density $\varepsilon\ge0$ and a smooth future unit timelike field $u$, including on $\{\varepsilon=0\}$. Set $\mathcal T=\varepsilon u^\flat\otimes u^\flat$ and require both $\nabla_u u=0$ and $u(\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\nabla_a u^a=0$ everywhere. Complete data are $(\varepsilon_0,U_0)$, with $\varepsilon_0\ge0$ and prescribed smooth future unit bundle velocity $U_0$, equivalently arbitrary smooth subluminal tilt. On positive-density regions this is [[def-gr-dust-matter-model]] with its density parameter equal to $\varepsilon$. Through empty regions the geodesic velocity is separately prescribed and matched; conservation of stress alone is not substituted for this full system. For a fixed $c>0$, the mass-normalized theorem [[thm-gr-dust-local-evolution]] applies with $\rho_0=\varepsilon_0/c^2$ and reconstructs $\varepsilon=c^2\rho$.

Require the constraints for the initial stress $T_0$ computed from this complete data on $\mathcal V$:
$$S_h+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T_0(\nu,\nu),\qquad \operatorname{div}_hK-d\operatorname{tr}_hK=\kappa T_0(\nu,\cdot).$$
These use the convention of [[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]. Equality of data includes equality of the model, constants, potential or EOS, and every component of $d$.

The local Cauchy-development and uniqueness suppliers for vacuum, scalar and strict fluid are the fixed-model theorem [[thm-gr-local-geometric-development]] and the two concrete branch theorems above. Its harmonic route requires the same fixed extraction/reconstruction rules and smooth symmetric-hyperbolic coefficient family for every compared physical solution, a positive time matrix on an admissible open state set, complete compatible initialization from $(h,K,d)$, propagation of auxiliary compatibility with recovery of the full matter equations on the reduced solution, and stress conservation on that reduced solution before Einstein recovery. These are the three explicit hypotheses of that theorem; conservation alone does not supply a Cauchy evolution law. Dust uses its independent common-flow/parallel-frame initialization, hyperbolic reduction, subsidiary recovery and uniqueness of [[thm-gr-dust-local-evolution]], rather than being asserted to satisfy the harmonic metric-first-derivative matter contract. Countable Choice and Dependent Choice are carried wherever these local theorems are invoked. Every additional fixed coupled model must supply the same complete-data local existence, admissibility, recovery and uniqueness obligations before it is used. This definition makes no local or global existence assertion.

**(a) Development.** A **development** of this data is a tuple
$(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ consisting of:

1. a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$
   ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]);
2. a smooth embedding $j:\Sigma\to M$ whose image $j(\Sigma)$ is a spacelike
   embedded hypersurface ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]
   clause (a));
3. the smooth tensor fields $\psi$ of the fixed model over $M$;
4. the equations on $M$: $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa\,T_{ab}(g,\psi)$ with
   the Einstein tensor of $g$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]])
   and $E(g,\psi)=0$;
5. the initial condition on $j(\Sigma)$: $j(\Sigma)$ is a Cauchy set of
   $(M,g,N)$ in the sense of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]
   clause (c), that is, every inextendible causal curve of
   [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] meets $j(\Sigma)$ in exactly one
   parameter value;
6. the induced data: $j^*(g)=h$, the second fundamental form of $j$ with
   respect to the future unit normal equals $K$ in the convention
   $K(V,W)=g(\nabla_Vn,W)$ of
   [[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]], and
   the initial data of $\psi$ on $j(\Sigma)$ transported by $j$ equal $d$.

No completeness of $(M,g)$, no inextendibility of $M$, and no claim that the
equations hold beyond $M$ are part of the definition. Whether a development is
globally hyperbolic is not part of the definition either; by clause 5 it
follows from [[thm-gr-cauchy-surface-implies-globally-hyperbolic]].

**(b) Data-fixing isometry.** A **data-fixing isometry** between developments
$(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ and $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ of the same data is a smooth
diffeomorphism $\varphi:M\to M'$ such that

1. $\varphi^*(g')=g$;
2. $g'_{\varphi(p)}(d\varphi_pN_p,N'_{\varphi(p)})<0$ for every $p\in M$: the isometry carries the future cone of $N$ onto that of $N'$;
3. $\varphi\circ j=j'$;
4. $\varphi^*\psi'=\psi$, with the natural pullback action on every listed tensor type (and the inverse differential on contravariant slots). Equality includes every listed field, including the prescribed dust velocity at zero density.

**(c) Development embedding.** A **development embedding** of $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$
into $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ is a smooth map $\varphi:M\to M'$ that is a
diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $M'$ and satisfies clauses (b)1-4.
Development embeddings are isometric immersions by clause (b)1.

**(d) Maximality.** A development $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ of the given data is
**maximal** when for every development $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ of the same data
there exists a development embedding $\varphi:M'\to M$. A maximal development
is also called a **maximal globally hyperbolic development** of the data.

**(e) Scope.** This is a mathematical definition of the solution class used by
the Cauchy problem. The physical reading of $(M,g,N)$ and $\psi$ and the
status of $(h,K,d)$ as initial data of a model of nature are supplied by
the framework postulates of the physics library, not here; and no existence,
uniqueness or maximality assertion is made by this definition.

Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ and $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ be two developments of the same
data in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]].

**(a) Common subdevelopment.** A **common subdevelopment** of $M$ and $M'$ is
a pair $(U,\varphi)$ in which

1. $U\subseteq M$ is an open subset with $j(\Sigma)\subseteq U$ such that the
   restriction $(U,g|_U,N|_U,j,\psi|_U)$ is a development of the same data
   (with the induced field equations on the open submanifold $U$); and
2. $\varphi:(U,g|_U,N|_U,j,\psi|_U)\to(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ is a development
   embedding in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]]
   clause (c).

Here "the induced field equations on $U$" means the equations of clause (a)4
of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] restricted to $U$; the
induced Lorentzian manifold is $(U,g|_U)$ with the time orientation $N|_U$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(b) Maximal common development.** A common subdevelopment $(U^*,\varphi^*)$
is a **maximal common development** (MCD) of $M$ and $M'$ when for every
common subdevelopment $(U,\varphi)$ one has $U\subseteq U^*$ and
$\varphi^*|_U=\varphi$. Existence is not asserted by this definition; it is
proved in [[lem-gr-maximal-common-development]].

**(c) Corresponding boundary points.** Let $(U,\varphi)$ be a common
subdevelopment. Its **corresponding boundary points** are pairs
$(p,p')\in\partial^M U\times\partial^{M'}\varphi(U)$, where the boundaries are
taken in $M$ and in $M'$ respectively, such that for every open neighbourhood
$V$ of $p$ in $M$ and every open neighbourhood $V'$ of $p'$ in $M'$ there is
$x\in V\cap U$ with $\varphi(x)\in V'$.

**(d) Side of the initial surface.** For a corresponding pair $(p,p')$: if
$V,V'$ range over a base of neighbourhoods, the condition of (c) forces every
$x$ witnessing it to lie on one side of $j(\Sigma)$: either $x\in I^+(j(\Sigma))$
for cofinally many witnesses, or $x\in I^-(j(\Sigma))$ for cofinally many
witnesses, but not both, since $I^\pm(j(\Sigma))$ are open and determined by
the trichotomy of [[lem-gr-cauchy-set-topology-and-graph]]. The corresponding
pair is then said to lie to the **future** or to the **past** of the initial
surface; the future case is the one used in this batch, the past case being
its time reverse.

**(e) Scope.** These are mathematical relations between two fixed developments
and their boundary points. Neither the existence of boundary points, nor the
existence of a common subdevelopment with nonempty boundary, nor uniqueness of
a corresponding point, is asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ and $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ be developments of the same
data in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause
(a), with $\Sigma:=j(\Sigma)$ and $\Sigma':=j'(\Sigma)$. Let
$\varphi:M\to M'$ be a smooth map with $\varphi^*(g')=g$, with
$g'_{\varphi(p)}(d\varphi_pN_p,N'_{\varphi(p)})<0$ for every $p\in M$, with
$\varphi\circ j=j'$ and $\varphi^*\psi'=\psi$ (so $\varphi$ is a future isometric immersion fixing the complete data and matching every matter field).
Then:

**(a)** $d\varphi_p:T_pM\to T_{\varphi(p)}M'$ is an isomorphism for every
$p\in M$;

**(b)** $\varphi$ is injective, hence a diffeomorphism onto the open subset
$\varphi(M)\subseteq M'$ and therefore a development embedding in the sense of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (c);

**(c)** if $M$ is connected and $\psi_1,\psi_2:M\to M'$ are two such
data-fixing isometric immersions, then $\psi_1=\psi_2$; in particular every
data-fixing self-isometry of a connected development is the identity of $M$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ and $(M',g',N',j',\psi')$ be developments of the same data
in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a),
with $\Sigma:=j(\Sigma)$. Then there exist $U^*\subseteq M$ and
$\psi^*:U^*\to M'$ such that:

**(a)** $(U^*,\psi^*)$ is a common subdevelopment of $M$ and $M'$ in the sense
of [[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]] clause (a);

**(b)** for every common subdevelopment $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ and $M'$ one has
$U\subseteq U^*$ and $\psi^*|_U=\varphi$; in particular $(U^*,\psi^*)$ is a
maximal common development in the sense of clause (b) of that definition, and
it contains $j(\Sigma)$;

**(c)** uniqueness: if $(U^\dagger,\psi^\dagger)$ also satisfies (a) and (b),
then $U^\dagger=U^*$ and $\psi^\dagger=\psi^*$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and suppose there exists a Cauchy set
$S\subseteq M$ ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause
(c)): every inextendible causal curve meets $S$ in exactly one parameter
value. Then:

**(a)** there is no nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
(so $(M,g,N)$ is causal and chronological in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (a));

**(b)** $(M,g,N)$ is strongly causal (clause (b) of that definition);

**(c)** for all $p,q\in M$ the causal diamond
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is globally
hyperbolic in the sense of clause (c) of that definition.

**Data.** Fix $\kappa>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, a smooth three-manifold $\Sigma$ without boundary, a smooth Riemannian metric $h$ and smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $K$. The normal convention is $K(V,W)=g(\nabla_Vn,W)$ for the future unit normal. Specify one fixed covariant matter model, consisting of a finite list of smooth tensor fields $\psi$, fixed equations $\mathcal E(g,\psi)=0$ and a fixed stress expression $\mathcal T(g,\psi)$, with pullback by local diffeomorphisms commuting with the equations and stress. Fix its complete smooth Cauchy data $d$: these determine all independent matter initial variables, not only the normal stress projections. Initial tensors with normal directions are specified on the abstract bundle $\mathcal V=\mathbb R\nu\oplus T\Sigma$ with metric $g_0(a\nu+X,b\nu+Y)=-ab+h(X,Y)$. In a development, identify $a\nu+X$ with $an+dj(X)$.

An admissible fixed coupled model is one satisfying the complete initialization, hyperbolic reduction, recovery and comparison hypotheses of [[thm-gr-local-geometric-development]], or a specified independent local existence and uniqueness reduction such as the dust branch below. The same fixed model, complete data and admissibility conditions are used in every comparison and at every restart. Admissibility includes the applicability of its supplied complete-data local existence and geometric uniqueness theorem to the data realized on each spacelike restart surface of the compared solutions. This must be checked for the actual model and surface; it is not inferred from stress conservation. This class includes the following four concrete branches; they do not exhaust it.

1. **Vacuum:** no matter fields, $\mathcal T=0$, and empty matter data.
2. **Scalar field:** fix one smooth potential $V$ and one normalization $K_\phi>0$. The field is $\varphi$, its equation is $\Box_g\varphi-V'(\varphi)=0$, its stress is the expression in [[def-gr-scalar-field-matter-model]] clause (c), and its complete data are $(\varphi_0,\pi_0)$ with $\pi_0=n(\varphi)|_\Sigma$. The fixed potential has no sign restriction ([[thm-gr-scalar-field-local-evolution]]).
3. **Strict barotropic fluid:** fix a smooth EOS $P:J\to\mathbb R$ on an open interval with $\epsilon+P(\epsilon)>0$ and $0<P'(\epsilon)<1$. The fields are $\epsilon\in J$ and future unit velocity $u$, the stress is $(\epsilon+P(\epsilon))u^\flat\otimes u^\flat+P(\epsilon)g$, and the equations are the continuity and Euler equations of [[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]] clause (c), with this fixed EOS. Complete data are $(\epsilon_0,v_0)$, where $\epsilon_0:\Sigma\to J$ and $h(v_0,v_0)<1$, equivalently the bundle velocity $U_0=(1-h(v_0,v_0))^{-1/2}(\nu+v_0)$. No small-tilt restriction is imposed ([[thm-gr-barotropic-fluid-local-evolution]]).
4. **Geodesic nonnegative dust:** the fields are an energy-coefficient density $\varepsilon\ge0$ and a smooth future unit timelike field $u$, including on $\{\varepsilon=0\}$. Set $\mathcal T=\varepsilon u^\flat\otimes u^\flat$ and require both $\nabla_u u=0$ and $u(\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\nabla_a u^a=0$ everywhere. Complete data are $(\varepsilon_0,U_0)$, with $\varepsilon_0\ge0$ and prescribed smooth future unit bundle velocity $U_0$, equivalently arbitrary smooth subluminal tilt. On positive-density regions this is [[def-gr-dust-matter-model]] with its density parameter equal to $\varepsilon$. Through empty regions the geodesic velocity is separately prescribed and matched; conservation of stress alone is not substituted for this full system. For a fixed $c>0$, the mass-normalized theorem [[thm-gr-dust-local-evolution]] applies with $\rho_0=\varepsilon_0/c^2$ and reconstructs $\varepsilon=c^2\rho$.

Require the constraints for the initial stress $T_0$ computed from this complete data on $\mathcal V$:
$$S_h+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T_0(\nu,\nu),\qquad \operatorname{div}_hK-d\operatorname{tr}_hK=\kappa T_0(\nu,\cdot).$$
These use the convention of [[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]. Equality of data includes equality of the model, constants, potential or EOS, and every component of $d$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $S\subseteq M$ be a Cauchy set
([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c)): every
inextendible causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ has
$\gamma^{-1}[S]=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$ of exactly one element. Then:

**(a)** there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\delta:[a,b]\to M$
with $\delta(a)=\delta(b)$; in particular $S$ is achronal and acausal, and
the three sets $I^-(S)$, $S$, $I^+(S)$ are pairwise disjoint with
$$M=I^-(S)\;\sqcup\;S\;\sqcup\;I^+(S);$$
moreover for $x\notin S$ one has $x\in I^+(S)$ if and only if some point of
$S$ chronologically precedes $x$;

**(b)** $S$ is closed in $M$;

**(c)** for every $p\in S$ there are a chart $(U,x)$ of the kind produced by
[[lem-gr-dominating-cone-bounds]] clauses (a) and (d) around $p$, with
$x(p)=0$ and the supplier constants $K\ge1$ and $c=16$, and numbers $a,\rho,\eta>0$ with $\sqrt c\,\rho+\eta<a$ and
$W:=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times B_\rho(0)\bigr)\subseteq U$ such that for every
$z\in B_\rho(0)$ the coordinate vertical line
$L_z=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times\{z\}\bigr)$ meets $S\cap W$ in exactly one
point $x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$, and
$$|\varphi(z)-\varphi(z')|\le\sqrt c\,|z-z'|\qquad(z,z'\in B_\rho(0)),$$
with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $|\varphi(z)|\le\sqrt c\,|z|<a$. The cylinder $W$ may be chosen inside any prescribed neighborhood of $p$. Consequently the maps
$z\mapsto x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$ form a topological atlas on the closed set
$S$, making $S$ a topological $3$-manifold in the subspace topology whose
inclusion into $M$ is a topological embedding.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let causal
curves be those of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Convergent ends are extendible.** Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the general absolutely continuous endpoint argument in this clause. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a future
causal curve and suppose $b:=\sup I<\infty$ and $\gamma(t)\to x\in M$ as
$t\to\sup I$. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a future causal curve
$\tilde\gamma$ defined on $I\cup[b,b+\varepsilon)$ whose restriction to $I$
is $\gamma$. Consequently a future-inextendible causal curve whose domain is
bounded above does not converge at its upper end, and the dual statement
holds at the past end.

**(b) Maximal geodesics have no limit.** Let $(p,v)\in TM$ with $v\ne0$ and
let $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$, as supplied by
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (a). Then
$\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ does not converge to any point of $M$ as $t\to\sup I_{p,v}$
or as $t\to\inf I_{p,v}$ (where convergence at an infinite end means
convergence as $t\to+\infty$ or $t\to-\infty$ respectively).

**(c) Segments lie on inextendible causal curves.** Let $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to M$
with $t_0<t_1$ be a future causal curve, or a past causal curve. Then there
is an inextendible causal curve $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ (same direction as
$\gamma$ in the case at hand) and a strictly increasing affine map
$\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to J$ with $\hat\gamma\circ\rho=\gamma$. In particular, any
two distinct points $p,q\in M$ with $p\le q$ and $p\ne q$ lie on a common
inextendible causal curve, and likewise for the past relation.

**(d) Cauchy sets are acausal.** Every Cauchy set of
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c) is acausal in
the sense of clause (b) of that definition.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $V\subseteq U\subseteq M$ be open
subsets with the induced metric and time orientation, and let
$\gamma:I\to U$ be a future causal curve
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]) that is inextendible in the
Lorentzian manifold $U$: $\gamma$ does not converge to any point of $U$ as its
parameter tends to either end of $I$ (clause (d) of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], read with ambient set $U$). Let $J$
be a connected component of
$$\gamma^{-1}[V]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in V\}.$$
Then $\gamma|_J$, regarded as a future causal curve in the Lorentzian manifold
$V$ with the restricted fields, is inextendible in $V$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ and the relations $\ll$, $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** if $p\ll q$ and $q\le r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(b)** if $p\le q$ and $q\ll r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(c)** if $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is a future causal curve and there are
$a\le s<t\le b$ such that $\gamma|_{[s,t]}$ is a future timelike curve, then
$\gamma(a)\ll\gamma(b)$;

**(d)** consequently
$$I^+\bigl(J^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega),\qquad I^-\bigl(J^-(\Omega)\bigr)=I^-(\Omega)$$
for every $\Omega\subseteq M$, and dually
$J^+\bigl(I^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega)$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Let $X$ be a set and write $\mathcal{P}(X)$ for its power set. A **topology** on
$X$ is a family $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ such that

- **(T1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$ and $X \in \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T2)** $\bigcup \mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{T}$ for every $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T3)** $U \cap V \in \mathcal{T}$ for all $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$.

A **topological space** is a pair $(X, \mathcal{T})$ consisting of a set $X$ and
a topology $\mathcal{T}$ on it; the elements of $X$ are its **points**. When only
one topology is in play we write $X$ for the pair; when several are, the topology
is always named.

The members of $\mathcal{T}$ are the **open** sets of $(X,\mathcal{T})$. A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed** when its complement $X \setminus F$ is open, and
**clopen** when it is both open and closed. By (T1) both $\varnothing$ and $X$
are clopen. *Open and closed are not opposites*: a set may be neither, and it may
be both, so "not open" is never a synonym for "closed".

**Finite intersections, and the empty one.** Axiom (T3) is stated for two sets
because that is all that is ever needed: if $n \ge 1$ and
$U_1, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{T}$, then $U_1 \cap \dots \cap U_n \in \mathcal{T}$
follows by iterating (T3) $n-1$ times. The intersection of the **empty** family
of subsets of $X$ is $X$, since the condition "lies in every member of the empty
family" is vacuous; that case is covered by (T1) rather than by (T3), which is
one of the two reasons $X \in \mathcal{T}$ is demanded outright. The other is
that (T2) alone gives only $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$.

**The closed sets, and the dual axiomatisation.** Put
$\mathcal{C} := \{\, X \setminus U : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\}$, the family of closed
sets. Then

- **(C1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{C}$ and $X \in \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C2)** $\bigcap \mathcal{D} \in \mathcal{C}$ for every **nonempty**
  $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C3)** $C \cup D \in \mathcal{C}$ for all $C, D \in \mathcal{C}$.

Conversely, if a family $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ satisfies (C1),
(C2) and (C3), then $\mathcal{T} := \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$
is a topology on $X$ whose closed sets are exactly the members of $\mathcal{C}$.
So a topology may be presented equally well by its open sets or by its closed
sets, and this library uses whichever is shorter.

*Both directions are one computation, and it is carried out here rather than
assumed.* The map $U \mapsto X \setminus U$ is an involution of
$\mathcal{P}(X)$, hence a bijection, and it carries the two De Morgan identities

$$X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing), \qquad X \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing)$$

term by term into each other. Given (T1)–(T3): $\varnothing = X \setminus X$ and
$X = X \setminus \varnothing$ lie in $\mathcal{C}$, which is (C1); for nonempty
$\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ the family
$\mathcal{S} = \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{D} \,\}$ lies in $\mathcal{T}$
and $\bigcap \mathcal{D} = X \setminus \bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is closed by (T2),
which is (C2); and $C \cup D = X \setminus ((X \setminus C) \cap (X \setminus D))$
is closed by (T3), which is (C3). Given (C1)–(C3) the same three lines run
backwards, the empty-union case $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$ being supplied
by (C1) rather than by (C2); and $\{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$ has
$\mathcal{C}$ as its family of complements because complementation is an
involution.

**Comparison of topologies.** If $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ are
topologies on the same set $X$ and $\mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_2$, then
$\mathcal{T}_1$ is **coarser** than $\mathcal{T}_2$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ is
**finer** than $\mathcal{T}_1$; the comparison is **strict** when the inclusion
is. Inclusion is a partial order on the set of topologies on $X$
([[def-partial-order]]), and it is not a total one: two topologies on the same
set may be incomparable.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
globally hyperbolic time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), and let
$t$ be the volume time function of [[thm-gr-volume-time-function]]. Then
there exist a smooth function $T:M\to\mathbb R$ and, with $\nabla T$ the
gradient of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], the
following hold.

**(a)** $T$ is a temporal function in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (e): smooth,
$g(\nabla T,\nabla T)<0$ and $g(\nabla T,N)>0$ everywhere.

**(b)** Every level set $S_c:=T^{-1}(c)$, $c\in\mathbb R$, is a Cauchy
hypersurface ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clauses (a)
and (c)): it is a spacelike embedded hypersurface and every inextendible
causal curve meets it in exactly one parameter value. In particular $T$ is
surjective.

**(c)** Along every inextendible future-directed causal curve
$T\to+\infty$, and along every inextendible past-directed causal curve
$T\to-\infty$.

**(d)** The vector field $X:=\nabla T/g(\nabla T,\nabla T)$ is smooth,
future-directed timelike, satisfies $X(T)=1$, and is complete
([[def-complete-vector-field]]): every maximal integral curve of $X$ is
defined on all of $\mathbb R$, so by
[[prop-a-vector-field-is-complete-if-and-only-if-its-flow-is-global]] its
flow $\Phi:\mathbb R\times M\to M$ is a global smooth flow
([[def-local-and-global-flow]]).

**(e)** The map $\Psi:\mathbb R\times S_0\to M$, $\Psi(s,z):=\Phi(s,z)$, is
a diffeomorphism and $T(\Psi(s,z))=s$ for all $(s,z)$; equivalently $M$ is
foliated by the Cauchy hypersurfaces $S_c$, each flow line meeting each level
exactly once.

**(f)** Put $\beta:=-1/g(\nabla T,\nabla T)$, a smooth positive function, and
$h_T:=g+\beta\,dT\otimes dT$. Then $g=-\beta\,dT\otimes dT+h_T$;
$h_T(X,\cdot)=0$; and $h_T$ restricted to $\ker dT$ is a smooth Riemannian
metric, so the decomposition $T_pM=\mathbb RX_p\oplus\ker dT_p$ is
$g$-orthogonal with $g(X,X)=-\beta$. Consequently the pullback of $g$ by the
diffeomorphism $\Psi$ has no mixed terms,
$$\Psi^*g=-(\beta\circ\Psi)\,ds^2+h,\qquad h_{(s,z)}(v,w):=g_{\Phi(s,z)}\bigl((d\Phi_s)_zv,(d\Phi_s)_zw\bigr),$$
a sum of a negative definite one-dimensional form and the smooth family of
Riemannian metrics induced on the levels.
