Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the global causal structure and auxiliary-length calculus used below.

Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ be a development of the given data
([[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)), write
$\Sigma:=j(\Sigma)$, and let $U_1,U_2\subseteq M$ be open with
$\Sigma\subseteq U_1\cap U_2$ such that $(U_i,g|_{U_i},N|_{U_i},j,\psi|_{U_i})$
is a development of the same data for $i=1,2$
([[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]] clause (a), with
the identity as the embedding where it is defined; equivalently, both $U_i$
carry restricted development structures over the same initial embedding $j$).
Then $(U_1\cap U_2,g|_{U_1\cap U_2},N|_{U_1\cap U_2},j,\psi|_{U_1\cap U_2})$ is
a development of the same data.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
geodesics, their maximal domains $I_{q,v}$ and the exponential maps
$\exp_q$ be those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Fix
$p\in M$. Write $\pi:TM\to M$ for the bundle projection.

**(a) Smoothness of the joint map.** The set
$$\mathcal D:=\{(q,v)\in TM:\ 1\in I_{q,v}\}\subseteq TM$$
is open in $TM$, and the **joint exponential map**
$$\Phi:\mathcal D\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Phi(q,v):=(q,\exp_q v),$$
is smooth.

**(b) Differential at $(p,0)$.** The differential $d\Phi_{(p,0)}$ is an
isomorphism. Explicitly, fix a smooth chart $(U,x)$ around $p$; it induces
the chart $(TU,Tx)$ of $TM$ and the product chart $(U\times U,x\times x)$ of
$M\times M$, and under the induced identifications
$T_{(p,0)}(TM)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ and
$T_{(p,p)}(M\times M)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ one has
$$d\Phi_{(p,0)}(u,w)=(u,\ u+w)\qquad\text{for all }u,w\in T_pM .$$

**(c) Diffeomorphism and two-point inverse.** There are open neighborhoods
$V\subseteq\mathcal D$ of $(p,0)$ and $W\subseteq M\times M$ of $(p,p)$ such
that $\Phi|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Moreover $V$ can be chosen
product-like: there are a chart $(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$, a radius
$r>0$ and a velocity radius $\rho>0$ such that, writing $B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb
R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$,
$$V=\bigl\{(q,v):\ q\in x^{-1}(B_r),\ \text{the coordinate components of }v\text{ in }(TU,Tx)\text{ lie in }B_\rho\bigr\},$$
and there is $s\in(0,r)$ with $x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$.
Consequently the velocity map
$$v:W\longrightarrow TM,\qquad (q,r)\longmapsto v(q,r):=\text{the vector with }(q,v(q,r))\in V,\ \Phi(q,v(q,r))=(q,r),$$
is well defined and smooth, and $\exp_q\bigl(v(q,r)\bigr)=r$ for all
$(q,r)\in W$.

**(d) Lipschitz bound for the two-point inverse.** On every pair
$x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$ as in (c) there is a constant
$\Lambda\ge 0$ such that, for all $q,r\in x^{-1}(B_s)$,
$$|v(q,r)|_x\le\Lambda\,\bigl|x(q)-x(r)\bigr|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $|v|_x$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate components of
$v$ and $v(q,q)=0$. In particular $|v(q,r)|_x\le 2\Lambda s$ on this pair.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) and geodesics as in
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $p\in M$ and let
$O\subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood of $p$. Then there are a chart
$(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$ and a radius $r>0$ such that
$C:=x^{-1}(B_r)$, $B_r=\{y\in\mathbb R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<r\}$ based at
$0=x(p)$, is contained in $O$ and has the following properties.

**(a) Normal neighborhood of each point.** For every $q\in C$ define
$$W_q:=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal E_q:\ \exp_q(tu)\in C\ \text{for every }t\in[0,1]\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal E_q$ is the exponential domain of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (d). Then $W_q$ is an
open star-shaped neighborhood of $0$ in $T_qM$, and
$\exp_q|_{W_q}:W_q\to C$ is a diffeomorphism onto $C$.

**(b) Unique contained joining segment.** For all $q,q'\in C$ there is
exactly one geodesic segment joining $q$ to $q'$ whose image is contained in
$C$, namely
$$x_{q,q'}:[0,1]\to C,\qquad x_{q,q'}(t)=\exp_q\bigl(t\,v(q,q')\bigr),$$
where $v(q,q')$ is the two-point inverse velocity of
[[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clause (c). For $q\ne q'$ the
points $x_{q,q'}(t)$, $0<t<1$, lie in $C$ strictly inside the coordinate
ball, i.e. $|x(x_{q,q'}(t))|_{\mathrm e}<r$; and $x_{q',q}$ is the time
reverse of $x_{q,q'}$ up to affine reparametrization.

**(c) Strict convexity.** In the terminology of
[[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b), $C$ is a
strictly convex normal neighborhood; in particular the position vector
$P(q,q')=d(\exp_q)_{v(q,q')}\bigl(v(q,q')\bigr)$ and the squared
displacement $D^2(q,q')=g_q\bigl(v(q,q'),v(q,q')\bigr)$ are defined for all
$q,q'\in C$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$. For every $x\in M$ there is an open
neighborhood $B$ of $x$, a strictly convex normal ball satisfying the
hypotheses of [[thm-gr-normal-neighborhood-causal-cone]] with base point
$x$, such that, writing $J_B(x)$, $I_B(x)\subseteq B$ for the endpoints in
$B$ of future causal, respectively future timelike, curves with image in
$B$ starting at $x$, and $\mathcal C^+,\mathcal T^+,\mathcal N^+$ for the
future causal or zero, future timelike, and future null nonzero vectors of
$\exp_x^{-1}(B)$:

**(a)** $J_B(x)=\exp_x(\mathcal C^+)$, $I_B(x)=\exp_x(\mathcal T^+)$, and
$J_B(x)\setminus(I_B(x)\cup\{x\})=\exp_x(\mathcal N^+)$;

**(b)** $J_B(x)$ and $J_B(x)\setminus I_B(x)$ are closed in $B$ and
$I_B(x)$ is open in $B$;

**(c)** there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\gamma:[0,1]\to B$
with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=x$;

**(d) corner smoothing.** if $\gamma:[0,1]\to B$ is future causal with
$\gamma(0)=x$ and there is $t_0$ at which $\gamma'(t_0)$ is future
timelike, then $\gamma(1)\in I_B(x)$;

**(e) closed relation at fixed base.** if $q_n\in J_B(x)$ and
$q_n\to q\in B$, then $q\in J_B(x)$; the same holds for the other two
sets of (a) in place of $J_B(x)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ and the chart $x=\psi_p$ on $T_0M$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.
Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every second countable space is separable.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of at most countable sets
([[def-countable]]) indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Then

$$U = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$$

is at most countable.

**The hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is not decoration and it is not removable.**
It is spent at exactly one step, step 3.1 below, where one surjection
$\mathbb{N} \to A_n$ is selected for every $n$ at once. Each $A_n$ has such
surjections, in general many of them, and the countability assumption provides no
rule for singling one out. Without some choice principle the theorem is not
available at all: ZF alone does not prove it, **conditionally on the consistency
of ZF**, as recorded on the later foundations page
`symmetric-collapse-and-ultrafilter-free-models-examples`. The
consistency hypothesis is not a formality and cannot be dropped: the separation
rests on an external independence result that this library quotes rather than
proves, and it cannot be stated without it.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

A family $\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ is a **basis for $\mathcal{T}$** if
every open set is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$: for every
$U \in \mathcal{T}$ there is $\mathcal{B}_U \subseteq \mathcal{B}$ with
$U = \bigcup \mathcal{B}_U$. Equivalently, and this is the form used in proofs,

$$\text{for every } U \in \mathcal{T} \text{ and every } x \in U \text{ there is } B \in \mathcal{B} \text{ with } x \in B \subseteq U .$$

*The two forms say the same thing.* If every open $U$ is such a union and
$x \in U$, then $x$ lies in one of the sets united, which is a member of
$\mathcal{B}$ inside $U$. Conversely, if the displayed condition holds then
$U = \bigcup \{\, B \in \mathcal{B} : B \subseteq U \,\}$, since each such $B$ is
contained in $U$ and each $x \in U$ lies in one of them. Note that
$\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$, so the empty open set is covered by the empty
subfamily and needs no member of $\mathcal{B}$. The members of a basis are called
**basic open sets**.

**The topology generated by a family.** Let $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$
be *any* family of subsets of $X$. Then

$$\langle \mathcal{S} \rangle := \bigcap \{\, \mathcal{T}' : \mathcal{T}' \text{ is a topology on } X \text{ with } \mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}' \,\}$$

is a topology on $X$, it contains $\mathcal{S}$, and it is contained in every
topology on $X$ that contains $\mathcal{S}$. It is called the **topology
generated by $\mathcal{S}$**, and $\mathcal{S}$ is a **subbasis** for a topology
$\mathcal{T}$ when $\mathcal{T} = \langle \mathcal{S} \rangle$.

*This is well posed, and the obligation is discharged here.* The collection being
intersected is nonempty, because $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is a topology on $X$ containing
$\mathcal{S}$; so the intersection is an intersection of a nonempty family of
subsets of $\mathcal{P}(X)$ and is a set. It is a topology: $\varnothing$ and $X$
lie in every topology on $X$, hence in the intersection, which is (T1); if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \langle \mathcal{S} \rangle$ then $\mathcal{S}'$ is a
subfamily of each $\mathcal{T}'$ in the collection, so $\bigcup \mathcal{S}'$ lies
in each $\mathcal{T}'$ and hence in the intersection, which is (T2); and the same
argument with $U \cap V$ gives (T3). It contains $\mathcal{S}$ because every
$\mathcal{T}'$ in the collection does, and it is contained in each such
$\mathcal{T}'$ because an intersection is contained in each of its members. So
$\langle \mathcal{S} \rangle$ is the coarsest topology on $X$ containing
$\mathcal{S}$ ([[def-topological-space]]), and in particular it is uniquely
determined by $\mathcal{S}$.

**Neither notion is intrinsic to the family alone.** "$\mathcal{B}$ is a basis
for $\mathcal{T}$" and "$\mathcal{S}$ is a subbasis for $\mathcal{T}$" are
relations between a family and a topology, not properties of the family. The
question of which families are a basis *for some* topology, and how the topology
generated by a subbasis is computed from it, is settled by the next item.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

before.claim: (Clause (a).) Each member is determined by four subsets of fixed sets as in [L1], so separation makes $\mathcal X$ a set; it is nonempty whenever some development of the data exists, by transporting that development through the flow representation [L6] (this transport is carried out in the proof of clause (e) below and uses no new hypothesis).

(Clause (e).) Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ be a development of the data; by [L4] it is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j(\Sigma)$. Let $T$ and $X$ be as in [L6] and $\Phi$ the global flow of $X$. For $x\in j(\Sigma)$ and $t\in\mathbb R$ the curve $s\mapsto\Phi(s,x)$ is a complete timelike integral curve; it cannot converge at any end, since $T(\Phi(t,x))=T(x)+t$ tends to $\pm\infty$ while a limit point would have finite $T$ by continuity ([L6]). Hence it is an inextendible timelike curve and meets the Cauchy surface $j(\Sigma)$ in exactly one parameter value; since it contains $x=\Phi(0,x)$, that value is $0$. Therefore $$\chi:\ D\longrightarrow M,\qquad D:=\{(x,t)\in j(\Sigma)\times\mathbb R:\ \Phi(s,x)\text{ defined for all }s\text{ between }0\text{ and }t\},\qquad \chi(x,t):=\Phi(t,x),$$ is bijective, with $D$ an open neighbourhood of $j(\Sigma)\times\{0\}$ (the flow domain is open), and smooth; it is a diffeomorphism because it is a smooth bijection whose differential is invertible: in the representation $M\cong\mathbb R\times T^{-1}(0)$ of [L6] clause (e), $\chi$ corresponds to $(c,z,t)\mapsto(c+t,z)$, a shear. Pulling back $g,N,\psi$ along $\chi$ and identifying $j(\Sigma)\cong\Sigma$ gives a tuple $(D,\chi^*g,\chi^*N,\chi^*\psi)\in\mathcal X$, and $\chi^{-1}:M\to D\subseteq Q$ is a data-fixing isometry onto its image; it is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of the member $D$ and satisfies $\chi^{-1}\circ j=j_0$, so it is a data-fixing development embedding of $M$ into $Q$. This proves (e).

(Clause (b): transitivity of the pairwise identifications.) Let $p\in U_\alpha$, $q\in U_\beta$, $r\in U_\gamma$ with $p\sim q$ via $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q\sim r$ via $\varphi_{\beta\gamma}$. Then $p\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p)\in U_{\beta\gamma}$, so $p\in V=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}(U_{\beta\gamma})$, and by [L3] the pair $(V,\chi)$ is a common subdevelopment of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ mapping $p$ to $\chi(p)=\varphi_{\beta\gamma}(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p))=r$. By the maximality property of the maximal common development of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$, $V\subseteq U_{\alpha\gamma}$ and $\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}(p)=\chi(p)=r$. Hence the identification of $p$ with $r$ holds at chain length two, and by induction at every finite chain length; the converse inclusion is the definition of the generating relations. This proves (b).

(Clause (c): the member maps and Hausdorffness.) By [L5] the map $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is continuous; it is injective because two points of $U_\alpha$ with the same class are identified by a chain which, by step 2.2, reduces to a single pairwise identification inside $U_\alpha$, and these identifications have the identity as their first coordinate ([[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]]: a common subdevelopment is realised inside its first member, and the map is injective by [[lem-gr-data-fixing-immersion-is-embedding]]). Openness: the saturation of an open $A\subseteq U_\alpha$ is the union over $\gamma\in\mathcal X$ of $\{x\in U_\gamma:\ x\sim a	ext{ for some }a\in A\}$, which by step 2.2 equals $$ igcup_{\gamma\in\mathcal X}\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}^{-1} igl(A\cap U_{\alpha\gamma} igr),$$ a union of open sets, because each $\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}$ is a diffeomorphism onto the open set $\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}(U_{\alpha\gamma})$ and $A\cap U_{\alpha\gamma}$ is open. Hence each $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is a homeomorphism onto the open set $Q_\alpha$, and the $Q_\alpha$ cover $Q$ because every class has a representative. For Hausdorffness let $[p]
e[q]$ with $p\in U_\alpha$, $q\in U_ eta$. Consider the pair quotient $Q_{\alpha eta}$ of [L2] with its canonical map $\kappa:Q_{\alpha eta}	o Q$; by step 2.2 the classes of $p$ and $q$ are distinct in $Q_{\alpha eta}$ (otherwise they would be identified by a chain, hence by the single pairwise identification), and $Q_{\alpha eta}$ is Hausdorff, so there are disjoint open $O_p
i[p]$, $O_q
i[q]$ in $Q_{\alpha eta}$. The map $\kappa$ is injective (step 2.2), continuous and open (the saturation argument above applies to the two-member family), hence a homeomorphism onto its open image; thus $\kappa(O_p),\kappa(O_q)$ are disjoint open neighbourhoods of $[p],[q]$ in $Q$. This proves (c).

(Clause (d): smooth structure and fields.) The charts of the members composed with the inverses of the homeomorphisms $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ provide an atlas on $Q$; transition functions between charts of the same member are smooth, and between charts of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on the common part $Q_\alpha\cap Q_\beta=\pi(U_{\alpha\beta})$ (step 2.2) they are of the form $\phi_\beta\circ\varphi_{\alpha\beta}\circ\phi_\alpha^{-1}$, which is smooth because $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image ([L2]). This yields a smooth atlas in which all $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ are diffeomorphisms onto open subsets, unique as a maximal atlas with this property. Whether $Q$ is second countable is a separate question, not decided here. The metric, time orientation and matter fields descend by pushforward along the $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$: the prescriptions for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ agree on the overlap because $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ is a data-fixing isometry ([L2]), and smoothness, Lorentzian signature and time orientation are local; the field equations are local and hold in each member, hence on $Q$; and $\bar j=\pi|_{U_\alpha}\circ j_0$ is well defined (the classes of $j_0(\Sigma)$ coincide by [L2]) and is an embedding with the induced data, since each $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is a data-fixing isometry. This proves the first part of (d).

(Clause (d): the Cauchy property, at least one meeting.) Let $\gamma:\bar I\to Q$ be a causal curve inextendible in $Q$ and pick $t_0\in\bar I$ with $\gamma(t_0)\in Q_\alpha$. Let $J$ be the connected component of $\gamma^{-1}[Q_\alpha]$ containing $t_0$. By [L4] the restriction $\gamma|_J$ is inextendible in the open set $Q_\alpha$, so its pullback under the diffeomorphism $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is a causal curve in $U_\alpha$ inextendible in $U_\alpha$; by [L4] it meets $j_0(\Sigma)$ in exactly one parameter value, so $\gamma$ meets $\bar j(\Sigma)$.

(Clause (d): at most one meeting.) Suppose $\gamma(t_1),\gamma(t_2)\in\bar j(\Sigma)$ with $t_1<t_2$; taking $t_1,t_2$ consecutive among the meetings of $\gamma$ with $\bar j(\Sigma)$: the set of meeting parameters is closed, and it is discrete, because near a meeting point the spacelike hypersurface $\bar j(\Sigma)$ is the zero set of a function with timelike gradient ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]), so the derivative of that function along the causal curve has a constant nonzero sign almost everywhere near the meeting and the composed function is strictly monotone there, giving at most one meeting in a small parameter interval; a closed discrete set ordered in $\mathbb R$ with two elements has consecutive elements, we may assume $\gamma(t)\notin\bar j(\Sigma)$ for $t_1<t<t_2$. The image $\gamma([t_1,t_2])$ is compact and covered by the open sets $Q_\alpha$, so finitely many members $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ cover it. If $\gamma([t_1,t_2])\subseteq Q_{\alpha_1}$, the segment lifts to a causal curve in $U_{\alpha_1}$ whose values at $t_1,t_2$ lie on $j_0(\Sigma)$; by [L4] it lies on an inextendible causal curve of $U_{\alpha_1}$, which would meet the Cauchy surface $j_0(\Sigma)$ in two parameter values, a contradiction. Otherwise set $R:=\bigcap_{i=1}^nU_{\alpha_1\alpha_i}$, an open neighbourhood of $j_0(\Sigma)$ in $U_{\alpha_1}$ which is a development of the data by the intersection lemma [[lem-gr-intersection-of-developments]] applied successively to the subdevelopments $U_{\alpha_1\alpha_i}$ of $U_{\alpha_1}$; by step 2.2, $\bigcap_{i=1}^nQ_{\alpha_i}=\pi(R)$. Now $\gamma(t_1),\gamma(t_2)\in\bar j(\Sigma)\subseteq\pi(R)$. If $\gamma([t_1,t_2])\subseteq\pi(R)$, the segment lifts to a causal curve in the development $R$ with two parameter values on its Cauchy surface, a contradiction. Otherwise choose a connected component $J^*$ of $\gamma^{-1}[\pi(R)]$ with $J^*\subsetneq[t_1,t_2]$, which exists because the preimage is open, contains both endpoints and is not everything. At each end of $J^*$ the curve immediately leaves $\pi(R)$ (maximality of the component), so $\gamma|_{J^*}$ does not converge to any point of the open manifold $\pi(R)$ at either end: it is inextendible in $\pi(R)\cong R$. By the Cauchy property of the development $R$ ([L4]) it meets $\bar j(\Sigma)$ at some parameter $s_0\in J^*\subseteq(t_1,t_2)$, contradicting the consecutiveness of $t_1,t_2$. Hence there is exactly one meeting.

after.claim: (Clause (a).) Each member is determined by four subsets of fixed sets as in [L1], so separation makes $\mathcal X$ a set; it is nonempty whenever some development of the data exists, by transporting that development through the flow representation [L6] (this transport is carried out in the proof of clause (e) below and uses no new hypothesis).

(Canonical representation of an arbitrary development.) Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ be a development. By [L4] it is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j(\Sigma)$. Let $X,\Phi,T$ be as in [L6]. Each integral curve is defined on $\mathbb R$ and satisfies $T(\Phi(t,y))=T(y)+t$, so it has no endpoint in $M$ and meets $j(\Sigma)$ exactly once. The map $\chi:\Sigma\times\mathbb R\to M$, $\chi(x,t)=\Phi(t,j(x))$, is therefore bijective and smooth. At $(x,t)$ its differential sends tangent vectors from $\Sigma$ to $d\Phi_t(dj(T_x\Sigma))$ and the time direction to $X_{\Phi(t,j(x))}=d\Phi_t(X_{j(x)})$. Since $j(\Sigma)$ is spacelike, $X_{j(x)}$ is not tangent to it; since $\Phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{-t}$, these images span $T_{\chi(x,t)}M$. Thus $\chi$ is a bijective local diffeomorphism, hence a diffeomorphism. Pulling back the metric, orientation representative and matter fields gives a tuple on $Z_0=\Sigma\times\mathbb R$ in $\mathcal X$, with $\chi\circ j_0=j$. This proves nonemptiness from the assumed development. The associated quotient embedding will be concluded after the quotient structure is established.

(Clause (b): transitivity of the pairwise identifications.) The identity common development of a member with itself gives $U_{\alpha\alpha}=U_\alpha$ and $\varphi_{\alpha\alpha}=\operatorname{id}$ by maximality [L2]; reversing a common-development embedding gives the same identifications in the opposite order, by the same maximality. Let $p\in U_\alpha$, $q\in U_\beta$, $r\in U_\gamma$ with $p\sim q$ via $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q\sim r$ via $\varphi_{\beta\gamma}$. Then $p\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p)\in U_{\beta\gamma}$, so $p\in V=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}(U_{\beta\gamma})$, and by [L3] the pair $(V,\chi)$ is a common subdevelopment of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ mapping $p$ to $\chi(p)=\varphi_{\beta\gamma}(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p))=r$. By the maximality property of the maximal common development of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$, $V\subseteq U_{\alpha\gamma}$ and $\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}(p)=\chi(p)=r$. Hence the identification of $p$ with $r$ holds at chain length two, and by induction at every finite chain length; the converse inclusion is the definition of the generating relations. This proves (b).

(Clause (c): the member maps and Hausdorffness.) By [L5] the map $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is continuous; it is injective because step 2.1 reduces any identification of points in $U_\alpha$ to the maximal common development with itself, which is $(U_\alpha,\operatorname{id})$ by the identity common development and maximality [L2]. Openness: the saturation of an open $A\subseteq U_\alpha$ is the union over $\gamma\in\mathcal X$ of $\{x\in U_\gamma:\ x\sim a	ext{ for some }a\in A\}$, which by step 2.1 equals $$ igcup_{\gamma\in\mathcal X}\varphi_{\alpha\gamma} igl(A\cap U_{\alpha\gamma} igr),$$ a union of open sets, because each $\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}$ is a diffeomorphism onto the open set $\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}(U_{\alpha\gamma})$ and $A\cap U_{\alpha\gamma}$ is open. Hence each $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is a homeomorphism onto the open set $Q_\alpha$, and the $Q_\alpha$ cover $Q$ because every class has a representative. For Hausdorffness let $[p]
e[q]$ with $p\in U_\alpha$, $q\in U_ eta$. Consider the pair quotient $Q_{\alpha eta}$ of [L2] with its canonical map $\kappa:Q_{\alpha eta}	o Q$; by step 2.1 the classes of $p$ and $q$ are distinct in $Q_{\alpha eta}$ (otherwise they would be identified by a chain, hence by the single pairwise identification), and $Q_{\alpha eta}$ is Hausdorff, so there are disjoint open $O_p
i[p]$, $O_q
i[q]$ in $Q_{\alpha eta}$. The map $\kappa$ is injective (step 2.1), continuous and open (the saturation argument above applies to the two-member family), hence a homeomorphism onto its open image; thus $\kappa(O_p),\kappa(O_q)$ are disjoint open neighbourhoods of $[p],[q]$ in $Q$. This proves (c).

(The local smooth structure, fields and future cones.) Compose the charts of each member with $(\pi|_{U_\alpha})^{-1}$. On $Q_\alpha\cap Q_\beta=\pi(U_{\alpha\beta})$, the transitions use the smooth data-fixing diffeomorphism $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$, so these charts generate a unique maximal compatible smooth atlas. The metrics and matter fields agree on overlaps and descend to $\bar g,\bar\psi$; the field equations hold locally. The pushforwards of $N_\alpha$ need not agree as vectors, but they select the same future timelike component on every overlap because $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ preserves future cones. Thus there is a consistent locally smooth choice of future cones, before any global representative field is asserted. The maps $\pi|_{U_\alpha}\circ j_0$ agree and define an embedded spacelike $S:=\bar j(\Sigma)$ with the prescribed induced data, since every member contains this entire surface and each member map is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset.

(A countable dense set without assuming second countability of $Q$.) Choose a countable dense $D_0\subseteq S$. At every newly occurring point choose one tangent basis and retain it at all later stages; let $R_x$ be its rational span. Recursively set $D_{n+1}=D_n\cup\{\exp_xv:x\in D_n, v\in R_x, \bar g_x(v,v)<0, \exp_xv\text{ defined}\}$ and $D=\bigcup_nD_n$. These sets are countable by [L9], using the declared choice axioms for the recursion. To show density, take $p\in Q_\alpha$ and its member flow line from $z_0\in S$ to $p$ given by [L6]. If its flow parameter is zero, density of $D_0$ in $S$ suffices. Otherwise partition its compact segment into finitely many nonconstant timelike subsegments, each contained in a convex normal neighborhood within this member. Write their endpoints $z_0,\ldots,z_k=p$. For negative flow parameter the chords are past timelike; for positive parameter they are future timelike. We show inductively $z_i\in\overline{D\cap Q_\alpha}$: if $z_{i-1}$ has this property, choose $d\in D\cap Q_\alpha$ sufficiently near $z_{i-1}$. In the local two-point inverse the vector $v(d,z_i)$ is timelike by continuity and openness of the timelike set. Approximate it by a timelike $u\in R_d$ so closely that the member geodesic remains defined to time one and $\exp_du$ lies in any prescribed neighborhood of $z_i$ within $Q_\alpha$. Such $u$ exists by rational density and openness of the local exponential domain. If $d\in D_m$, then $\exp_du\in D_{m+1}\subseteq D$, with no claim that $m=i-1$. The exact inverse satisfies $\exp_d(v(d,z_i))=z_i$; no approximation error is added for this equality. This proves the induction and density of $D$ in $Q$.

(An explicit countable basis.) In each fixed tangent basis at $d\in D$, let $B_d(a,r)$ denote a Euclidean ball with rational center $a\in\mathbb Q^4$ and rational radius $r>0$. Form the family of all $\exp_d(B_d(a,r))$ for which the ball lies in the exponential domain and $\exp_d$ restricts to a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $Q$. This family is countable by [L9] and consists of open sets by its definition. Given $p\in O$ with $O$ open, choose a member containing $p$ and use its joint exponential inverse near $(p,p)$. For all $d$ in a sufficiently small open neighborhood of $p$ in that member, there is a velocity $v(d,p)$ inside an open fiber domain $H_d$ on which $\exp_d$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open set containing $p$. Choose such $d\in D$ by step 5.1. The open set $H_d\cap\exp_d^{-1}(O)$ contains $v(d,p)$, so a rational translated ball in the fixed basis at $d$ contains $v(d,p)$ and lies in this open set. Its image is a family member containing $p$ and contained in $O$. This proves the basis criterion and hence second countability of $Q$.

(A smooth global orientation representative.) The quotient is now a smooth manifold in the full sense of [L10]. Choose a subordinate locally finite smooth partition of unity $(\rho_\alpha)$ for the member cover and put $\bar N=\sum_\alpha\rho_\alpha(\pi|_{U_\alpha})_*N_\alpha$, extending each summand by zero outside $Q_\alpha$. Each summand is smooth because its support lies in $Q_\alpha$; the sum is locally finite. At every point the nonzero summands are positive multiples of vectors in the same future timelike component by step 4.1 and at least one coefficient is positive since the coefficients sum to one. Cone convexity makes $\bar N$ smooth, nowhere zero and future timelike. Every member map therefore preserves time orientation in the sense of preserving future cones. The metric and matter fields are the descended fields of step 4.1; the particular representative $\bar N$ is not claimed unique.

(Clause (d): the Cauchy property, at least one meeting.) Let $\gamma:\bar I\to Q$ be a causal curve inextendible in $Q$ and pick $t_0\in\bar I$ with $\gamma(t_0)\in Q_\alpha$. Let $J$ be the connected component of $\gamma^{-1}[Q_\alpha]$ containing $t_0$. By [L4] the restriction $\gamma|_J$ is inextendible in the open set $Q_\alpha$, so its pullback under the diffeomorphism $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is a causal curve in $U_\alpha$ inextendible in $U_\alpha$; by [L4] it meets $j_0(\Sigma)$ in exactly one parameter value, so $\gamma$ meets $\bar j(\Sigma)$.

(Compatible side decomposition.) In each member write $U_\alpha=I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)\sqcup j_0\Sigma\sqcup I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)$ as in [L4]. For $x\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ the side computed in $U_{\alpha\beta}$ is the same as in $U_\alpha$: a timelike curve inside the subdevelopment gives membership in the corresponding ambient side, and these sides are disjoint. The isometry $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ identifies these subdevelopment sides with those in its image in $U_\beta$, so the side in $U_\beta$ is identical. It follows that $Q^-:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ and $Q^+:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ are disjoint open sets and $Q=Q^-\sqcup S\sqcup Q^+$. In particular $S$ is closed. A future causal segment in a member that starts on its Cauchy surface lies, immediately afterwards, in its future side, and one ending on the surface lies immediately beforehand in its past side: extend the segment to an inextendible causal curve in that member; the unique Cauchy meeting and the disjoint side decomposition give the stated sides. More explicitly, any future-side point before the meeting would yield a timelike curve from the surface followed by a causal segment back to it, contrary to acausality; the past-side case after the meeting is its time reverse, using the push-up rule underlying the member side decomposition.

(At most one Cauchy meeting.) Suppose a future causal curve $\gamma$ has two parameter values on $S$. In a member neighborhood of any meeting it can meet $S$ at most once, since $S$ is the member's acausal Cauchy surface. Thus its meeting parameters form a relatively closed locally discrete subset; on the compact interval between the proposed two meetings it is finite, and we may choose consecutive meetings $t_1<t_2$. The connected image $\gamma((t_1,t_2))$ misses $S$, so by step 8.2 it lies wholly in either $Q^-$ or $Q^+$. Near $t_1$ it lies in a member containing $\gamma(t_1)$, and the member side observation of step 8.2 puts it in $Q^+$. Near $t_2$ the same observation puts it in $Q^-$. This contradicts the disjointness of these sides. A past causal curve is treated by reversing its parameter. Together with step 8.1, every inextendible causal curve meets $S$ exactly once; all development conditions, including second countability, hold.

(Universality.) For an arbitrary development $M$, use its canonical representative $D:=\Sigma\times\mathbb R\in\mathcal X$ and diffeomorphism $\chi:D\to M$ from step 1.2. The map $(\pi|_D)\circ\chi^{-1}:M\to Q$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset, an isometry preserving future cones and matter fields, and takes $j$ to $\bar j$. Hence it is a data-fixing development embedding, proving (e).
(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish (a), step 2.1 establishes (b), step 3.1 establishes (c), steps 4.1-9.1 establish (d), and step 10.1 establishes (e).

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Fix the data of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]]: a smooth three-manifold
$\Sigma$ with smooth Riemannian metric $h$, smooth symmetric tensor $K$,
one fixed admissible covariant matter model with its complete smooth Cauchy
data $d$, and constants $\Lambda,\kappa$. The model and its complete data,
including all required initial derivatives and prescribed fields on empty
regions, are fixed throughout. Assume the supplied complete-data local
existence and geometric uniqueness hypotheses apply on every spacelike
restart surface occurring in comparisons, as required by that definition.
Assume that at least one development of these data exists.
Write $Z_0:=\Sigma\times\mathbb R$ and let $j_0:\Sigma\to Z_0$,
$j_0(x):=(x,0)$.

**(a) The set-sized family.** Let $\mathcal X$ be the collection of all
tuples $(U,g,N,\psi)$ such that $U\subseteq Z_0$ is an open neighbourhood of
$j_0(\Sigma)$ in $Z_0$, $g$ is a smooth Lorentzian metric on $U$, $N$ a time
orientation and $\psi$ matter fields of the sector on $U$, and
$(U,g,N,j_0,\psi)$ is a development of the data in the sense of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a). Then
$\mathcal X$ is a set, and it is nonempty provided at least one development
of the data exists.

**(b) Identifications.** For $\alpha=(U_\alpha,g_\alpha,N_\alpha,\psi_\alpha)$
and $\beta\in\mathcal X$ let $(U_{\alpha\beta},\varphi_{\alpha\beta})$ be
their maximal common development, regarded as a subset of $U_\alpha$
([[lem-gr-maximal-common-development]], [[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]];
in the convention of the definition it is realised inside the first member).
Let $Z:=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in\mathcal X}U_\alpha$ and let $\sim$ be the
equivalence relation on $Z$ **generated** by the relations
$x\sim\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(x)$ for $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal X$ and
$x\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ (a finite chain of such steps, in either order).
Then the classes of two points $p\in U_\alpha$, $q\in U_\beta$ coincide if and
only if $p\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p)$.

**(c) The quotient.** Let $Q:=Z/{\sim}$ with quotient map $\pi$. Then
$\pi|_{U_\alpha}:U_\alpha\to Q$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset
$Q_\alpha:=\pi(U_\alpha)$, the family $\{Q_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in\mathcal X}$
covers $Q$, and $Q$ is Hausdorff.

**(d) Structure.** $Q$ is a Hausdorff, second countable smooth four-manifold and carries a
unique smooth atlas (unique in the sense of maximal atlases compatible with
the charts below) making all maps $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ diffeomorphisms onto open
subsets, together with a smooth Lorentzian metric $\bar g$, a time orientation
$\bar N$ and matter fields $\bar\psi$ such that every $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is an
isometry onto its image preserving time orientation and matter fields, and
such that $\bar j:=\pi|_{U_\alpha}\circ j_0$ (independent of $\alpha$) is a
common embedding of $\Sigma$ with induced data $(h,K,d)$. The field
equations hold on $Q$, and every causal curve in $Q$ that is inextendible in
$Q$ meets $\bar j(\Sigma)$ in exactly one parameter value. Consequently
$(Q,\bar g,\bar N,\bar j,\bar\psi)$ is a development of the data
in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a).
The representative $\bar N$ is chosen to determine the common future cones;
it need not equal the pushforward of each representative $N_\alpha$.

**(e) Universality.** Every development $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ of the same data
admits a data-fixing development embedding into $Q$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (c).

step_quotes.quote: 1.1 (Clause (a).) Each member is determined by four subsets of fixed sets as in [L1], so separation makes $\mathcal X$ a set; it is nonempty whenever some development of the data exists, by transporting that development through the flow representation [L6] (this transport is carried out in the proof of clause (e) below and uses no new hypothesis). [L1, L6, algebra]

1.2 (Canonical representation of an arbitrary development.) Let $(M,g,N,j,\psi)$ be a development. By [L4] it is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $j(\Sigma)$. Let $X,\Phi,T$ be as in [L6]. Each integral curve is defined on $\mathbb R$ and satisfies $T(\Phi(t,y))=T(y)+t$, so it has no endpoint in $M$ and meets $j(\Sigma)$ exactly once. The map $\chi:\Sigma\times\mathbb R\to M$, $\chi(x,t)=\Phi(t,j(x))$, is therefore bijective and smooth. At $(x,t)$ its differential sends tangent vectors from $\Sigma$ to $d\Phi_t(dj(T_x\Sigma))$ and the time direction to $X_{\Phi(t,j(x))}=d\Phi_t(X_{j(x)})$. Since $j(\Sigma)$ is spacelike, $X_{j(x)}$ is not tangent to it; since $\Phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{-t}$, these images span $T_{\chi(x,t)}M$. Thus $\chi$ is a bijective local diffeomorphism, hence a diffeomorphism. Pulling back the metric, orientation representative and matter fields gives a tuple on $Z_0=\Sigma\times\mathbb R$ in $\mathcal X$, with $\chi\circ j_0=j$. This proves nonemptiness from the assumed development. The associated quotient embedding will be concluded after the quotient structure is established. [L6, L4, algebra]

5.1 (A countable dense set without assuming second countability of $Q$.) Choose a countable dense $D_0\subseteq S$. At every newly occurring point choose one tangent basis and retain it at all later stages; let $R_x$ be its rational span. Recursively set $D_{n+1}=D_n\cup\{\exp_xv:x\in D_n, v\in R_x, \bar g_x(v,v)<0, \exp_xv\text{ defined}\}$ and $D=\bigcup_nD_n$. These sets are countable by [L9], using the declared choice axioms for the recursion. To show density, take $p\in Q_\alpha$ and its member flow line from $z_0\in S$ to $p$ given by [L6]. If its flow parameter is zero, density of $D_0$ in $S$ suffices. Otherwise partition its compact segment into finitely many nonconstant timelike subsegments, each contained in a convex normal neighborhood within this member. Write their endpoints $z_0,\ldots,z_k=p$. For negative flow parameter the chords are past timelike; for positive parameter they are future timelike. We show inductively $z_i\in\overline{D\cap Q_\alpha}$: if $z_{i-1}$ has this property, choose $d\in D\cap Q_\alpha$ sufficiently near $z_{i-1}$. In the local two-point inverse the vector $v(d,z_i)$ is timelike by continuity and openness of the timelike set. Approximate it by a timelike $u\in R_d$ so closely that the member geodesic remains defined to time one and $\exp_du$ lies in any prescribed neighborhood of $z_i$ within $Q_\alpha$. Such $u$ exists by rational density and openness of the local exponential domain. If $d\in D_m$, then $\exp_du\in D_{m+1}\subseteq D$, with no claim that $m=i-1$. The exact inverse satisfies $\exp_d(v(d,z_i))=z_i$; no approximation error is added for this equality. This proves the induction and density of $D$ in $Q$. [step 4.1, L6, L8, L9, construct]

step_quotes.quote: 2.1 (Clause (b): transitivity of the pairwise identifications.) The identity common development of a member with itself gives $U_{\alpha\alpha}=U_\alpha$ and $\varphi_{\alpha\alpha}=\operatorname{id}$ by maximality [L2]; reversing a common-development embedding gives the same identifications in the opposite order, by the same maximality. Let $p\in U_\alpha$, $q\in U_\beta$, $r\in U_\gamma$ with $p\sim q$ via $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q\sim r$ via $\varphi_{\beta\gamma}$. Then $p\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p)\in U_{\beta\gamma}$, so $p\in V=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}(U_{\beta\gamma})$, and by [L3] the pair $(V,\chi)$ is a common subdevelopment of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ mapping $p$ to $\chi(p)=\varphi_{\beta\gamma}(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p))=r$. By the maximality property of the maximal common development of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$, $V\subseteq U_{\alpha\gamma}$ and $\varphi_{\alpha\gamma}(p)=\chi(p)=r$. Hence the identification of $p$ with $r$ holds at chain length two, and by induction at every finite chain length; the converse inclusion is the definition of the generating relations. This proves (b). [step 1.1, L3, algebra]

7.1 (A smooth global orientation representative.) The quotient is now a smooth manifold in the full sense of [L10]. Choose a subordinate locally finite smooth partition of unity $(\rho_\alpha)$ for the member cover and put $\bar N=\sum_\alpha\rho_\alpha(\pi|_{U_\alpha})_*N_\alpha$, extending each summand by zero outside $Q_\alpha$. Each summand is smooth because its support lies in $Q_\alpha$; the sum is locally finite. At every point the nonzero summands are positive multiples of vectors in the same future timelike component by step 4.1 and at least one coefficient is positive since the coefficients sum to one. Cone convexity makes $\bar N$ smooth, nowhere zero and future timelike. Every member map therefore preserves time orientation in the sense of preserving future cones. The metric and matter fields are the descended fields of step 4.1; the particular representative $\bar N$ is not claimed unique. [step 4.1, step 6.1, L10, construct]

9.1 (At most one Cauchy meeting.) Suppose a future causal curve $\gamma$ has two parameter values on $S$. In a member neighborhood of any meeting it can meet $S$ at most once, since $S$ is the member's acausal Cauchy surface. Thus its meeting parameters form a relatively closed locally discrete subset; on the compact interval between the proposed two meetings it is finite, and we may choose consecutive meetings $t_1<t_2$. The connected image $\gamma((t_1,t_2))$ misses $S$, so by step 8.2 it lies wholly in either $Q^-$ or $Q^+$. Near $t_1$ it lies in a member containing $\gamma(t_1)$, and the member side observation of step 8.2 puts it in $Q^+$. Near $t_2$ the same observation puts it in $Q^-$. This contradicts the disjointness of these sides. A past causal curve is treated by reversing its parameter. Together with step 8.1, every inextendible causal curve meets $S$ exactly once; all development conditions, including second countability, hold. [step 8.1, step 8.2, contradiction, algebra]

([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Fix the data of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]]: a smooth three-manifold
$\Sigma$ with smooth Riemannian metric $h$, smooth symmetric tensor $K$,
one fixed admissible covariant matter model with its complete smooth Cauchy
data $d$, and constants $\Lambda,\kappa$. The model and its complete data,
including all required initial derivatives and prescribed fields on empty
regions, are fixed throughout. Assume the supplied complete-data local
existence and geometric uniqueness hypotheses apply on every spacelike
restart surface occurring in comparisons, as required by that definition.
Assume that at least one development of these data exists.
Write $Z_0:=\Sigma\times\mathbb R$ and let $j_0:\Sigma\to Z_0$,
$j_0(x):=(x,0)$.

**(a) The set-sized family.** Let $\mathcal X$ be the collection of all
tuples $(U,g,N,\psi)$ such that $U\subseteq Z_0$ is an open neighbourhood of
$j_0(\Sigma)$ in $Z_0$, $g$ is a smooth Lorentzian metric on $U$, $N$ a time
orientation and $\psi$ matter fields of the sector on $U$, and
$(U,g,N,j_0,\psi)$ is a development of the data in the sense of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a). Then
$\mathcal X$ is a set, and it is nonempty provided at least one development
of the data exists.

**(b) Identifications.** For $\alpha=(U_\alpha,g_\alpha,N_\alpha,\psi_\alpha)$
and $\beta\in\mathcal X$ let $(U_{\alpha\beta},\varphi_{\alpha\beta})$ be
their maximal common development, regarded as a subset of $U_\alpha$
([[lem-gr-maximal-common-development]], [[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]];
in the convention of the definition it is realised inside the first member).
Let $Z:=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in\mathcal X}U_\alpha$ and let $\sim$ be the
equivalence relation on $Z$ **generated** by the relations
$x\sim\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(x)$ for $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal X$ and
$x\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ (a finite chain of such steps, in either order).
Then the classes of two points $p\in U_\alpha$, $q\in U_\beta$ coincide if and
only if $p\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ and $q=\varphi_{\alpha\beta}(p)$.

**(c) The quotient.** Let $Q:=Z/{\sim}$ with quotient map $\pi$. Then
$\pi|_{U_\alpha}:U_\alpha\to Q$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset
$Q_\alpha:=\pi(U_\alpha)$, the family $\{Q_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in\mathcal X}$
covers $Q$, and $Q$ is Hausdorff.

**(d) Structure.** $Q$ is a Hausdorff, second countable smooth four-manifold and carries a
unique smooth atlas (unique in the sense of maximal atlases compatible with
the charts below) making all maps $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ diffeomorphisms onto open
subsets, together with a smooth Lorentzian metric $\bar g$, a time orientation
$\bar N$ and matter fields $\bar\psi$ such that every $\pi|_{U_\alpha}$ is an
isometry onto its image preserving time orientation and matter fields, and
such that $\bar j:=\pi|_{U_\alpha}\circ j_0$ (independent of $\alpha$) is a
common embedding of $\Sigma$ with induced data $(h,K,d)$. The field
equations hold on $Q$, and every causal curve in $Q$ that is inextendible in

$(Q,\bar g,\bar N,\bar j,\bar\psi)$ is a development of the data
in the sense of [[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a).

it need not equal the pushforward of each representative $N_\alpha$.

admits a data-fixing development embedding into $Q$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (c).

The map $\chi:\Sigma\times\mathbb R\to M$, $\chi(x,t)=\Phi(t,j(x))$, is therefore bijective and smooth. At $(x,t)$ its differential sends tangent vectors from $\Sigma$ to $d\Phi_t(dj(T_x\Sigma))$ and the time direction to $X_{\Phi(t,j(x))}=d\Phi_t(X_{j(x)})$. Since $j(\Sigma)$ is spacelike, $X_{j(x)}$ is not tangent to it; since $\Phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{-t}$, these images span $T_{\chi(x,t)}M$. 8.2 (Compatible side decomposition.) In each member write $U_\alpha=I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)\sqcup j_0\Sigma\sqcup I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma)$ as in [L4]. For $x\in U_{\alpha\beta}$ the side computed in $U_{\alpha\beta}$ is the same as in $U_\alpha$: a timelike curve inside the subdevelopment gives membership in the corresponding ambient side, and these sides are disjoint. The isometry $\varphi_{\alpha\beta}$ identifies these subdevelopment sides with those in its image in $U_\beta$, so the side in $U_\beta$ is identical. It follows that $Q^-:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^-_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ and $Q^+:=\bigcup_\alpha\pi(I^+_\alpha(j_0\Sigma))$ are disjoint open sets and $Q=Q^-\sqcup S\sqcup Q^+$. In particular $S$ is closed. Near $t_1$ it lies in a member containing $\gamma(t_1)$, and the member side observation of step 8.2 puts it in $Q^+$. Near $t_2$ the same observation puts it in $Q^-$. This contradicts the disjointness of these sides. A past causal curve is treated by reversing its parameter.
